title: Hijack Execution Flow: Executable Installer File Permissions Weakness
shortTitle: Hijack Execution Flow: Executable Installer File Permissi...
summary: This sub-technique abuses weak permissions around installer processes. Installers commonly unpack their own files, such as libraries and helper programs, into a subdirectory of the temporary folder during a run, and when that directory or the unpacked binaries can be written by an ordinary user, an attacker can replace a file before the installer or one of its children executes it. The supplier's process then launches the attacker's binary, so the replacement inherits the privilege level of the installer, which may be the local system account. The same weakness applies to a legitimate binary in a program directory whose access control list is too permissive. The outcome is local privilege escalation when the installer runs on demand, or persistence when the affected process is scheduled, started at boot, or triggered by a system event. Detection centres on process creation records that show an installer, or a process it spawns, running a binary from a temporary or user writable path.

beginner.definition: An installer is a program that copies and sets up other software. Sometimes an installer unpacks files into a temporary folder first. If a normal user can write to that folder, an attacker can swap a file before it runs. The installer then executes the attacker's file, often with higher permissions.
beginner.whyItMatters: Installers often need deep access to change the system. That means their files run with strong permissions. If one of those files can be replaced, the attacker gains the same permissions. A normal user account can then reach the highest level on the machine. Checking folder permissions on installer paths prevents this quietly.
howItWorks: An installer starts and creates a working folder, usually inside the temporary directory.
It unpacks its own files, such as programs and libraries, into that folder.
If the folder permissions allow ordinary users to write, a file can be replaced.
The installer then launches the replaced file as part of its normal work.
The replacement runs with the permissions of the installer, which are often high.
If the installer runs on a schedule, the same trick repeats for persistence.
beginner.example: Imagine a moving company that packs your boxes in a shared loading bay. The bay is open, so anyone can reach the boxes. A stranger swaps one box for another with the same label. The movers carry it into your new home without checking the contents. Installer permission weaknesses work like that. The installer packs files in a folder other people can reach. If one file is swapped, the installer delivers it for the attacker.
takeaways: Installers unpack files, and those unpacked files must be protected.
A binary running from a temporary folder deserves a second look.
Review write permissions on installer and program directories.

objectives: Explain how weak installer file permissions can be abused.
Describe why a replaced file can run with higher privileges.
Explain how this sub-technique differs from the Hijack Execution Flow parent.
Identify the process creation and file write events that reveal the swap.
Describe how to review permissions on installer and program directories.
